# Generative video architecture index

Canonical B2 product documentation: <https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage-ai-machine-learning>.

Use this index to choose a workflow. Each linked architecture documents its data flow, B2 zones and security boundaries.

## [Ingest licensed footage, then split, caption and curate a text-to-video training corpus](../architectures/curate-video-training-corpus/architecture.md)

Licensed source video lands in an immutable raw bucket; curation engines split, score, filter, dedupe and caption it over the S3 API and write clips, captions, scores and embeddings back under run-addressed prefixes so each dataset version traces to the run that produced it.

- **Audience:** Video model data engineering teams, Dataset curation and licensing operations, Security and storage architects
- **Problem:** Curating TB-PB of source footage into tens to hundreds of millions of clips is slow and costly when footage is copied to every GPU node per pass, and without an immutable raw tier and per-run lineage nobody can later show which footage a model was trained on.
- **Workflow:** Bulk-load source footage with rclone or video2dataset into a raw bucket with licence sidecars → Store raw footage under write-once prefixes; apply Object Lock governance retention when required → Run GPU curation (Cosmos Curator, Daft or Pixeltable) directly against the raw bucket → Caption with a VLM and ASR, then write clips, keyframes, captions and score tables to a curated bucket by run ID → Store clip embeddings in a Lance table for dedupe and semantic lookup → Publish per-run stats, the recipe config and a dataset card that lists run IDs and thresholds
- **Integrations:** rclone, video2dataset, NVIDIA Cosmos Curator, Daft, Pixeltable, LanceDB / Lance
- **Keep off B2:** URL frontier and download-status queue (Postgres, Redis or Spark state); Rights and licence database; Ray or Slurm task state; GPU-local decode scratch; In-RAM FAISS index used during dedupe; Run-tracking database
- **Expected scale:** TB-PB of source footage, many millions of derived clips, highly parallel ranged reads during decode. Standard B2 is the default; consider B2 Overdrive only after measurement shows sustained object-store throughput, not GPU decode, limits curation passes.

## [Stream video shards into distributed diffusion training and version checkpoints and LoRAs](../architectures/stream-shards-train-video-diffusion/architecture.md)

Curated clips or precomputed latents are packed into immutable versioned shards that stream from B2 into multi-node GPU training; checkpoints, LoRAs, samples and eval metrics return to B2 so preempted jobs resume, and approved weights are promoted to a model prefix for inference.

- **Audience:** Video model training and ML platform engineers, GPU cluster operators across neoclouds, Security and storage architects
- **Problem:** Video diffusion transformers train on tens to hundreds of TB of shards across many GPUs and emit multi-GB checkpoints, so the data and checkpoint tier must be reachable from any cluster, survive preemption, and record lineage from dataset version to released weights.
- **Workflow:** Pack clips or latents into WebDataset, MDS or LitData shards under a new versioned prefix with an index → Benchmark shard size and dataloader worker count against B2 before a large run → Stream shards into training with MosaicML Streaming, LitData or a WebDataset s3 opener → Write checkpoints through Ray Train storage_path or Composer save_folder → Log samples, metrics and LoRAs to MLflow or a ZenML artifact store, or as W&B reference artifacts → Promote approved weights to the models bucket (download with a read-only checkpoint key, re-upload with the publisher key), then expire intermediate checkpoints by age
- **Integrations:** MosaicML Streaming, Lightning LitData, Ray Train, MosaicML Composer checkpointing, MLflow, ZenML, Weights & Biases reference artifacts
- **Keep off B2:** Node-local NVMe shard cache and dataloader shuffle buffers; In-memory checkpoint staging and NCCL state; Experiment-tracking backend database (MLflow or W&B metadata); Scheduler and job queue; Dataset registry database that maps versions to runs
- **Expected scale:** Tens to hundreds of TB of shards read concurrently by many GPU workers; multi-GB checkpoints written on a fixed cadence. Benchmark shard size and worker count against B2 first. Standard B2 is the default; B2 Overdrive may apply when sustained multi-node read throughput is the measured bottleneck.

## [Run a self-hosted open-weight video diffusion farm with shared weights and outputs](../architectures/self-hosted-video-diffusion-farm/architecture.md)

Ephemeral ComfyUI GPU workers pull shared video diffusion checkpoints, VAEs and LoRAs from a model bucket with ETag-validated caching, render clips, and save outputs with the workflow JSON and seed to a generation prefix, returning presigned sharing URLs.

- **Audience:** Generative media platform engineers, Creative studios running open-weight models, GPU fleet operators
- **Problem:** Video diffusion weights run 5-30+ GB per checkpoint and GPU workers are ephemeral across clouds, so re-downloading from the Hugging Face Hub on every cold start wastes GPU time and outputs on worker disk vanish with the instance.
- **Workflow:** Mirror the Hugging Face cache into models/hf-cache/ with hf-cache-sync → Store custom checkpoints, LoRAs and VAEs under models/{family}/{version}/ → Version ComfyUI workflow graphs under workflows/ and inputs under inputs/ → Render and save outputs with workflow JSON and seed to renders/ → Share outputs through time-limited presigned GET URLs and expire scratch/ by lifecycle
- **Integrations:** ComfyUI Cloud Storage nodes, HF Cache Sync
- **Keep off B2:** Hot weights in GPU VRAM and on worker NVMe; Job queue (Redis, SQS or Temporal); User, session and billing database; Worker scratch frames during a render
- **Expected scale:** Few large weight objects read on every cold start; many small-to-medium video outputs written per job. ETag-validated local caching avoids repeat downloads; Standard B2 is the default and Overdrive is unlikely to matter unless a large fleet cold-starts at once.

## [Generate video across hosted model APIs and keep every output with a provenance manifest](../architectures/hosted-multi-provider-generation-provenance/architecture.md)

A prompt becomes a storyboard and keyframes that fan out to hosted text-to-video and image-to-video APIs; every intermediate and final asset is copied into B2 before the provider URL expires, with a per-run manifest of SHA-256 hashes, provider, model, prompt, params, seed and parent_run_id.

- **Audience:** Generative media application developers, Teams comparing hosted video model providers, Trust, safety and legal reviewers
- **Problem:** Hosted video APIs return expiring result URLs and charge per generation, so a lost take costs another generation; provider comparison, disclosure and takedown all need a provider-neutral, unchanged record of what produced each asset.
- **Workflow:** Upload references to inputs/ with an explicit Content-Type; relay them to upload APIs (Runway) or hand them over as short-lived presigned GET URLs (Replicate) → Application workers orchestrate storyboard, keyframes, image-to-video, TTS and music through the chosen providers → Sink outputs to runs/{tenant}/{date}/{run_id}/ as soon as each provider returns them (Replicate keeps API outputs for one hour by default) → Store the run manifest with outputs and parent_run_id for linked pipelines → A separate audit publisher copies approved manifests to an Object Lock bucket where retention must be provable → Replay or fork runs from manifests and review takes through presigned URLs
- **Integrations:** Runway API, Replicate
- **Keep off B2:** Provider API keys (secrets manager); Job queue; User, tenant and billing database; Search index over manifest metadata; C2PA or manifest signing keys (KMS or HSM)
- **Expected scale:** Many short generation runs, each producing tens of small-to-medium assets plus one manifest. Throughput is bounded by provider latency, not storage; Standard B2 fits and Overdrive does not apply.

## [Moderate, review and approve generated video before it is published](../architectures/moderate-review-approve-generated-video/architecture.md)

New clips land in a staging prefix; a B2 Event Notification triggers safety classification and a manifest hash check, editors review in a MAM connected to the same bucket, approved masters are copied to a published location, flagged assets move to quarantine, and disputed assets go under legal hold.

- **Audience:** Trust and safety engineering teams, Post-production and MAM administrators, Legal and compliance reviewers
- **Problem:** Generated video must pass policy, brand and legal checks before release, and copying it between moderation systems, MAM tools and archives creates divergent copies that break the audit trail disclosure and takedown requests depend on.
- **Workflow:** Generators write to inbox/staging/; a B2 Event Notification posts a signed webhook to an event broker → A moderation worker samples and classifies frames, writes reports to inbox/moderation/ and moves violations to inbox/quarantine/ → A verifier recomputes SHA-256 and compares it with the run manifest → Editors review passing assets in iconik with proxies built from a bucket scan → Approved masters are server-side copied to published/ and the staging copy is hidden; disputed assets get a legal hold
- **Integrations:** iconik (Backlight), EditShare FLOW
- **Keep off B2:** Moderation review queue and reviewer database; MAM metadata databases (iconik, FLOW); Takedown ticketing; Signing keys; Event broker subscriber registry
- **Expected scale:** Event-driven, per-asset processing; moderation compute scales with generation volume. Storage throughput is rarely the bottleneck; Standard B2 fits.

## [Finish, transcode and deliver generated video through a CDN](../architectures/finish-package-deliver-generated-video/architecture.md)

Approved generations get finishing passes (upscale, interpolation, matting, captions, cutdowns) recorded in job manifests, are transcoded to HLS ladders, posters and WebVTT, and are served from B2 through a CDN partner or a signing edge app; managed video platforms ingest masters from presigned URLs.

- **Audience:** Generative media product engineers, Video delivery and streaming engineers, FinOps and storage architects
- **Problem:** Many gen-video models emit short, low-resolution, low-frame-rate clips that need finishing, and each master fans out into renditions with heavy read traffic, so egress fees and duplicate copies across render, transcode and CDN tiers dominate cost.
- **Workflow:** Run finishing jobs that write scratch frames and renders with JSON job manifests → Transcode masters into HLS renditions, posters, sprites and WebVTT with ffmpeg or Telestream Vantage → Serve delivery/ through Cloudflare, Fastly or bunny.net with Cache-Control set in bucket info → Hand masters to Mux with a presigned GET URL when managed playback is used → Expire scratch and intermediates by lifecycle; keep masters and only the latest version of each rendition
- **Integrations:** Cloudflare CDN / Workers, bunny.net CDN, Fastly, Telestream Vantage Gateway, Mux Video
- **Keep off B2:** CDN edge cache; Player analytics; Entitlement and auth service; Transcode and finishing job queue; Mux-hosted renditions when Mux handles playback
- **Expected scale:** Read-heavy delivery with many renditions per master; bursty finishing and transcode writes. CDN caching absorbs hot reads; Standard B2 is the origin default.
